Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Uffizi Gallery, Florence, Italy - Museum Tour

Stop 1: Leda col cigno

Coordinates: 43.7675, 11.2551

The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday from 8:15 to 6:30, and closed on Mondays. Admission is 25 euros for adults; under-18s go free.

Orientation: These three works span centuries yet share a common thread of mythological and biblical narratives. Your first stop is Leda col cigno. From three paces back, the surface of “Leda col cigno” reveals its gloss of oil on panel, and the size—130 by 77.5 centimeters—lets you see how the myth fills the vertical space: Leda and the swan almost life-sized, emerging against a backdrop that still breathes with Renaissance imagination.

The painting before you, an oil on panel created circa 1505–1507, is attributed to the circle of Leonardo da Vinci—possibly Francesco Melzi—after Leonardo’s own lost original. The oil technique, with its sheen and depth of color, draws the figures forward against the background. Leonardo da Vinci, working in Milan around 1510, was deeply engaged with the mythological theme of Leda and the Swan, and his exploration began as early as 1504 with sketches showing Leda kneeling, one arm around the swan. Melzi, Leonardo’s pupil, produced this copy, ensuring the master’s vision survived when the original was lost.

The commission of such mythological subjects reflected the Medici court’s appetite for scenes where the divine interrupts the human: Jupiter, transformed as a swan, and Leda, the queen of Sparta, caught in an intimate, ambiguous encounter. Upon arrival at the Uffizi, restorers replaced the head and added the right arm and parts of the robe, as well as the head and neck of the swan. These changes altered the original composition but allowed the work to endure. The story of “Leda col cigno” is one of transformation—both physical and conceptual—revealing the Renaissance fascination with boundaries: god and mortal, original and copy, creation and loss.

Directions: Continue through Uffizi Gallery — next is Adorazione dei Magi.

Stop 2: Adorazione dei Magi

Coordinates: 43.7675, 11.2551

Orientation: Stand directly before Leonardo da Vinci’s Adorazione dei Magi, close enough to trace the movement of his unfinished lines. From this vantage, the swirling energy of the composition—the tumult of figures, horses, and palms—emerges most vividly, revealing the underdrawing’s restless searching and the tension between chaos and revelation that fades at a distance.

In March 1481, the Augustinian monks of San Donato a Scopeto commissioned Leonardo da Vinci to paint an altarpiece of the Adoration of the Magi for their high altar. Leonardo began work on the large panel but left it unfinished when he departed Florence for Milan, leaving the abandoned painting behind. What you see before you is not a finished oil painting, but the raw, luminous beginning: tempera on wood, with the Christ Child and Virgin Mary at the center, the three Magi kneeling in homage, and a shifting multitude pressing toward the sacred moment. Leonardo’s hand is visible in the energetic, unresolved marks—faces half-emerged, horses rearing, and architectural ruins rising in the background. The underdrawing and monochrome wash reveal his working process—his search for movement, emotion, and meaning—preserved as if time itself stalled with his departure.

That same year, Lippi successfully finished his own altarpiece. The monks’ later decision to commission a new work from Lippi speaks to the rupture that Leonardo’s absence left in Florence’s artistic and religious life. This painting marks a pivotal turning point in Leonardo’s life. The cost was not only monetary or contractual, but spiritual—a moment of Florentine devotion left suspended, its promise unfulfilled.

Standing before this work, the viewer witnesses the birth of a new pictorial world: not the static serenity of earlier altarpieces, but a surging chaos out of which order and meaning struggle to emerge. The Magi—so venerated in Florence, and the subject of many commissions—are caught in a moment of recognition, the old and the new colliding in the unfinished energy of the scene. Here, the promise lies unresolved, asking what it means when creation halts—when, in the unfinished, the possibility of new worlds waits. The cycle of origin and fall, so central to human stories, finds new form in this suspended vision.

Your final stop in Uffizi Gallery: Adamo ed Eva.

Stop 3: Adamo ed Eva

Coordinates: 43.7675, 11.2551

Orientation: As you stand here before Lucas Cranach the Elder’s “Adamo ed Eva,” position yourself just a pace back from the center, so that Adam’s panel on the left and Eve’s on the right rise before you as distinct but intimately paired presences. From here, the difference in their heights—Adam at 172 by 63 centimeters, Eve at 167 by 61—becomes pronounced, and the delicate line that divides the two wooden panels sets up a tension: each figure alone, yet forever entwined. This vantage point also reveals a detail many miss: the peculiar winged serpent on Adam’s panel, an unsettling herald of transformation.

What you see is a double oil painting on wood, signed and dated 1528 by Lucas Cranach the Elder—his name inscribed on Adam’s panel, near the winged serpent. The serpent, its wings spread, becomes the agent of change: not only the biblical tempter but a marker of metamorphosis, as if something irretrievable has just been set in motion. When Cranach painted these panels in 1528, he was already a recognized master. This work marked his engagement with Italian painting, especially in his use of perspective and color. At this moment in his life, he was navigating the shifting tastes and allegiances of patrons on both sides of the Alps. In the seventeenth century, a Florentine biographer misattributed “Adamo ed Eva” to Albrecht Dürer. Standing before “Adamo ed Eva,” the tension is palpable—the echo of the transformation seen in the Adorazione dei Magi, now stripped to its elemental core.

Together, these works explore the theme of transformation—whether through mythological encounters, unfinished artistic endeavors, or the pivotal moments of biblical narratives. This fascination with change invites us to reflect on the nature of creation and the potential that lies within the unresolved.

That's 3 stops in all.
